title: University Physics I
description: Calculus-based University Physics I: measurement and vectors, kinematics, Newton's laws, work and energy, momentum and collisions, rotation, gravitation, oscillations, waves and sound, fluids, and thermodynamics. Assumes Calculus I (derivatives and integrals are used throughout).
author: Examiner
changelog: Checked against university, AP and open-textbook sources; corrected incomplete statements and constants, and added a few short sections; new lesson on damped and driven oscillations.

lessons.title: Measurement, units, and significant figures
lessons.body:
## Why physics starts with measurement

Physics makes claims you can test, and testing means measuring. Every physical quantity in this course is a number times a unit: "3.2 m" means 3.2 copies of the standard length called a meter. Drop the unit and the number means nothing, so a habit worth building on day one is to carry units through every line of every calculation. This lesson sets up three tools you will use in all the others: the SI unit system with its prefixes, the rules for honest precision (significant figures), and dimensional analysis, which catches mistakes before they cost you.

## SI units and prefixes

The international system (**[[SI units]]**) builds everything from seven base units. The four you will meet most are the meter (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, and the ampere (A) for current; the kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela complete the set. Every other unit is a **[[derived unit]]**, a product or quotient of base units. Speed is m/s, acceleration m/s², and the newton is defined so that $1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg·m/s}^2$ (it is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²). The joule is $1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N·m} = 1\text{ kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2$, and the watt is $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J/s}$.

Prefixes scale a unit by powers of ten:

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor | Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| giga | G | $10^{9}$ | centi | c | $10^{-2}$ |
| mega | M | $10^{6}$ | milli | m | $10^{-3}$ |
| kilo | k | $10^{3}$ | micro | μ | $10^{-6}$ |
| | | | nano | n | $10^{-9}$ |

Large and small values are written in **[[scientific notation]]**, $a \times 10^n$ with $1 \le |a| < 10$: the mass of an electron is $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, far easier to read than thirty zeros.

## Converting units

A **[[conversion factor]]** is a fraction equal to 1, such as $\dfrac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}}$. Multiplying by 1 changes nothing physical, so you may multiply by as many conversion factors as you like, choosing each one so that the unwanted unit cancels.

### Example 1

Convert a highway speed of 108 km/h to m/s.

Write the quantity, then multiply by factors that cancel km and h:

$$108\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \frac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}} \times \frac{1\text{ h}}{3600\text{ s}} = \frac{108\,000}{3600}\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} = 30\text{ m/s}.$$

Check: km cancels against km, h against h, leaving m/s. A useful shortcut follows: dividing km/h by 3.6 gives m/s.

When a unit is squared or cubed, the conversion factor must be squared or cubed too. Since $1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}$, we get $1\text{ cm}^2 = (10^{-2}\text{ m})^2 = 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$ and $1\text{ cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$. Forgetting to square the factor is the most common conversion error in the whole course.

### Example 2

A plate has area 250 cm². What is its area in m²?

$$250\text{ cm}^2 \times \left(\frac{1\text{ m}}{100\text{ cm}}\right)^2 = 250 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2 = 0.025\text{ m}^2.$$

If you had used $\tfrac{1}{100}$ instead of $\left(\tfrac{1}{100}\right)^2$ you would get 2.5 m², a plate the size of a dining table.

## Significant figures

No measurement is exact. A ruler marked in millimeters lets you read a length as 12.3 cm with the last digit estimated; writing 12.300 cm would claim precision you don't have. **[[Significant figures]]** (sig figs) are the digits that carry real information. The rules:

- Nonzero digits are significant: 4.56 has three.
- Zeros between nonzero digits are significant: 2.05 has three.
- Leading zeros only place the decimal point: 0.0071 has two.
- Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 3.400 has four.
- Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous: write 1200 as $1.2 \times 10^3$ (two) or $1.200 \times 10^3$ (four) to be clear.

Scientific notation removes every ambiguity, because all digits in $a$ are significant.

*Calculating with measured values.* The result can't be more reliable than the weakest input, but "weakest" means different things for different operations:

- *Multiplying or dividing*: keep as many sig figs as the input with the fewest sig figs.
- *Adding or subtracting*: keep as many decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places.

Exact numbers (counted objects, the 2 in $2\pi r$, defined conversions like 100 cm = 1 m) never limit precision. Round only at the end; carry an extra digit or two through intermediate steps.

### Example 3

A rectangle measures 4.52 m by 2.1 m. Report its area.

$4.52 \times 2.1 = 9.492$. The inputs have 3 and 2 sig figs, so the answer gets 2: area $= 9.5\text{ m}^2$.

Now add masses of 12.41 kg and 3.2 kg: $15.61$, but 3.2 is known only to tenths, so report 15.6 kg.

**[[Accuracy]]** and **[[precision]]** are different ideas. Accuracy is how close a result is to the true value; precision is how tightly repeated measurements cluster (and how many digits you can justify). A miscalibrated scale can be very precise and still inaccurate.

## Dimensional analysis

Every quantity has a **[[dimension]]**: length [L], mass [M], time [T], and so on. Speed has dimension [L]/[T], acceleration [L]/[T]², force [M][L]/[T]². **[[Dimensional analysis]]** rests on one fact: you can only add, subtract or equate quantities with the same dimension. So both sides of any correct equation must match dimensionally, term by term.

That gives a fast sanity test. Is $x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$ plausible? $[v_0 t] = \tfrac{L}{T}\cdot T = L$ and $[a t^2] = \tfrac{L}{T^2}\cdot T^2 = L$. Every term is a length, as $x$ is. If you derive $x = v_0 t^2$, the check fails ($[L][T]$), so you know an error crept in. The pure number $\tfrac12$ has no dimension, so dimensional analysis can't detect a wrong numerical factor; it catches wrong powers and missing quantities.

### Example 4

A pendulum's period $T$ might depend on its length $L$, the bob's mass $m$, and $g$ (dimension [L]/[T]²). Find the form of the relationship.

Suppose $T = C\,L^a m^b g^c$ with $C$ a pure number. Dimensions: $[T]^1 = [L]^a [M]^b [L]^c [T]^{-2c}$. Matching powers: mass gives $b = 0$; time gives $-2c = 1$, so $c = -\tfrac12$; length gives $a + c = 0$, so $a = \tfrac12$. Therefore $T = C\sqrt{L/g}$. The mass drops out, and the full theory later supplies $C = 2\pi$.

Arguments of functions like $\sin$, $e^x$ and $\ln$ must be dimensionless, which is another quick check: $e^{-t/\tau}$ makes sense only if $\tau$ is a time.

## Estimation and orders of magnitude

Physicists often estimate before calculating. An **[[order of magnitude]]** is the power of ten nearest a value: a person's mass (70 kg) is order $10^2$ kg. Rough estimates ("how many heartbeats in a lifetime?" about $70\text{ beats/min} \times 5\times10^5\text{ min/yr} \times 80\text{ yr} \approx 3\times10^9$) tell you whether a precise answer is reasonable.

## Units of derivatives and integrals

Units follow calculus operations naturally. A derivative $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ is a ratio of small changes, so its unit is (unit of $x$)/(unit of $t$): position in m gives velocity in m/s. An integral $\int f\,dt$ is a sum of products $f\,\Delta t$, so its unit is (unit of $f$)·(unit of $t$): integrating velocity (m/s) over time (s) gives meters. Keep this in mind when checking calculus-based formulas: $\int F\,dx$ has units N·m = J, which is why it can be an energy.

## Common mistakes

- Converting area or volume with an unsquared or uncubed factor (cm² to m² is $10^{-4}$, not $10^{-2}$).
- Dropping units midway and then guessing them at the end.
- Rounding intermediate results, so the final answer drifts.
- Applying the multiplication rule to addition (or the reverse).
- Treating "dimensionally correct" as "correct": a missing factor of 2 passes the check.

## Key points

- Every quantity is a number times a unit; SI base units include m, kg, s, A, K, mol.
- Convert by multiplying by factors equal to 1; square or cube them for areas and volumes.
- Multiply/divide: fewest sig figs. Add/subtract: fewest decimal places. Exact numbers don't count.
- Equations must be dimensionally consistent; function arguments must be dimensionless.
- Derivatives divide units; integrals multiply them.

lessons.title: Vectors
lessons.body:
## Quantities with direction

Some quantities are fully described by one number and a unit: mass, temperature, time, energy. These are **[[scalars]]**. Others need a direction as well: walking 3 km is not the same trip as walking 3 km north. A **[[vector]]** has a magnitude (size, never negative) and a direction. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum are all vectors, so nearly every mechanics problem in this course starts by handling vectors correctly.

We write vectors in bold or with an arrow, $\vec A$, and the magnitude as $|\vec A|$ or plain $A$. Geometrically, a vector is an arrow: its length is the magnitude and it points in its direction. Moving the arrow without rotating or stretching it gives the same vector.

## Adding vectors geometrically

To add $\vec A + \vec B$, place the tail of $\vec B$ at the head of $\vec A$; the **[[resultant]]** runs from the tail of $\vec A$ to the head of $\vec B$ (the tip-to-tail method). Order doesn't matter: $\vec A + \vec B = \vec B + \vec A$. To subtract, add the opposite: $\vec A - \vec B = \vec A + (-\vec B)$, where $-\vec B$ has the same length as $\vec B$ and points the opposite way.

```shape
{"segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [4, 0], "arrow": true, "label": "A"}, {"from": [4, 0], "to": [4, 3], "arrow": true, "label": "B"}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [4, 3], "arrow": true, "dashed": true, "label": "A + B"}], "caption": "Tip to tail: walk 4 units east, then 3 north; the resultant is 5 units long"}
```

Multiplying a vector by a scalar $c$ stretches it by $|c|$, and a negative $c$ also reverses it.

## Components

Drawing is good for intuition but poor for precision. Instead, we break a vector into **[[components]]** along perpendicular axes. If $\vec A$ has magnitude $A$ and makes angle $\theta$ with the $+x$ axis (measured counterclockwise),

$$A_x = A\cos\theta, \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta.$$

These come straight from the right triangle whose hypotenuse is $\vec A$. Components are signed numbers: a vector pointing into the second quadrant has $A_x < 0$ and $A_y > 0$.

Going back, the Pythagorean theorem and the tangent give

$$A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}.$$

Careful with the angle: a calculator's $\tan^{-1}$ returns values between $-90^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, so if $A_x < 0$ you must add $180^\circ$. Always sketch the vector to see which quadrant it's in.

With **[[unit vectors]]** $\hat\imath$ and $\hat\jmath$ (length 1, pointing along $+x$ and $+y$; $\hat k$ along $+z$), a vector is written $\vec A = A_x\hat\imath + A_y\hat\jmath$. Adding vectors then means adding components:

$$\vec A + \vec B = (A_x + B_x)\,\hat\imath + (A_y + B_y)\,\hat\jmath.$$

That works because addition is done separately along each independent direction.

### Example 1

A hiker walks 5.0 km at $30^\circ$ north of east, then 3.0 km due north. Find the total displacement.

Components of the first leg: $A_x = 5.0\cos 30^\circ = 4.33$ km, $A_y = 5.0\sin 30^\circ = 2.50$ km. Second leg: $B_x = 0$, $B_y = 3.0$ km.

Sum: $R_x = 4.33$ km, $R_y = 5.50$ km.

Magnitude: $R = \sqrt{4.33^2 + 5.50^2} = \sqrt{18.75 + 30.25} = 7.0$ km.

Direction: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(5.50/4.33) = 51.8^\circ$ north of east. Both components are positive, so the calculator angle is already in the right quadrant.

### Example 2

$\vec A = 3\hat\imath - 4\hat\jmath$ and $\vec B = -1\hat\imath + 2\hat\jmath$ (meters). Find $\vec C = 2\vec A - \vec B$ and its magnitude.

$2\vec A = 6\hat\imath - 8\hat\jmath$; subtracting $\vec B$ gives $\vec C = 7\hat\imath - 10\hat\jmath$ m. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{49 + 100} = \sqrt{149} \approx 12.2$ m, and it points $\tan^{-1}(-10/7) = -55^\circ$, that is, $55^\circ$ below the $+x$ axis.

## Choosing axes

Axes are your choice; physics doesn't care. Pick them to make the work easy. For a block on a ramp, tilt the axes so $x$ runs along the ramp: then the motion is along one axis and only gravity needs splitting. You will see this trick again in the friction lesson.

## Multiplying vectors: dot and cross products

There are two ways to multiply two vectors.

The **[[dot product]]** (scalar product) gives a number:

$$\vec A \cdot \vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z,$$

where $\phi$ is the angle between the vectors when placed tail to tail. It measures how much two vectors point the same way: it's positive for $\phi < 90^\circ$, zero for perpendicular vectors, negative for $\phi > 90^\circ$. The component form follows because $\hat\imath\cdot\hat\imath = 1$ and $\hat\imath\cdot\hat\jmath = 0$. Work, $W = \vec F \cdot \vec d$, is a dot product.

The **[[cross product]]** (vector product) gives a vector perpendicular to both:

$$|\vec A \times \vec B| = AB\sin\phi,$$

with direction set by the **[[right-hand rule]]**: point your fingers along $\vec A$, curl them toward $\vec B$, and your thumb points along $\vec A \times \vec B$. The cross product is anticommutative, $\vec B\times\vec A = -\vec A\times\vec B$. In components,

$$\vec A \times \vec B = \begin{vmatrix} \hat\imath & \hat\jmath & \hat k \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix} = (A_yB_z - A_zB_y)\hat\imath + (A_zB_x - A_xB_z)\hat\jmath + (A_xB_y - A_yB_x)\hat k.$$

Torque $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$ and the magnetic force $q\vec v \times \vec B$ (University Physics II) are cross products.

### Example 3

Find the angle between $\vec A = 2\hat\imath + 1\hat\jmath + 2\hat k$ and $\vec B = 1\hat\imath + 4\hat\jmath - 1\hat k$, and compute $\vec A \times \vec B$.

Dot product: $2(1) + 1(4) + 2(-1) = 4$. Magnitudes: $A = \sqrt{4+1+4} = 3$ and $B = \sqrt{1+16+1} = \sqrt{18} = 4.243$. So $\cos\phi = \dfrac{4}{3(4.243)} = 0.314$ and $\phi = 71.7^\circ$.

Cross product: $\hat\imath$ component $1(-1) - 2(4) = -9$; $\hat\jmath$ component $2(1) - 2(-1) = 4$; $\hat k$ component $2(4) - 1(1) = 7$. So $\vec A\times\vec B = -9\hat\imath + 4\hat\jmath + 7\hat k$. Check: its dot product with $\vec A$ is $-18 + 4 + 14 = 0$, so it is perpendicular to $\vec A$, as it must be.

Vectors can also be functions of time. Differentiating $\vec r(t) = x(t)\hat\imath + y(t)\hat\jmath$ component by component gives velocity, which is how 2D kinematics will work.

## Common mistakes

- Adding magnitudes instead of components: 3 m east plus 4 m north is 5 m, not 7 m.
- Using $\sin$ for the $x$ component when the angle is measured from the $x$ axis (or forgetting to swap when the angle is from the $y$ axis).
- Trusting $\tan^{-1}$ blindly when $A_x$ is negative.
- Mixing degree and radian mode on the calculator.
- Writing $\vec B \times \vec A$ for $\vec A\times\vec B$, which flips the sign.

## Key points

- Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction.
- $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ (angle from $+x$); $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$.
- Add vectors by adding components; choose axes that simplify the problem.
- $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi$ (a scalar); $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\phi$, direction by the right-hand rule.

lessons.title: Describing motion in one dimension
lessons.body:
## What kinematics is for

**[[Kinematics]]** describes motion, where things are and how fast that changes, without yet asking what causes it (that's Newton's laws, in the next module). We start with motion along a straight line, because everything in two and three dimensions is built from it one axis at a time. The vector ideas from the last lesson apply directly: in one dimension a vector is just a signed number, with the sign giving the direction.

## Position, displacement, and distance

Choose an origin and a positive direction. An object's **[[position]]** $x$ is its coordinate along that line. The **[[displacement]]** over a time interval is the change in position,

$$\Delta x = x_f - x_i,$$

which can be positive, negative or zero. **[[Distance]]** is the total length of path covered, always positive. Walk 5 m forward and 5 m back: distance 10 m, displacement 0.

## Velocity and speed

The **[[average velocity]]** over an interval is displacement divided by elapsed time:

$$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}.$$

**[[Average speed]]** is distance divided by time. They can differ wildly: a runner who finishes one lap of a 400 m track in 80 s has average speed 5 m/s but average velocity 0, since she ends where she started.

Average velocity hides what happened inside the interval. Shrink the interval and you approach the **[[instantaneous velocity]]**, the velocity at one moment, which is what a speedometer reports (its magnitude is the instantaneous speed).

### Example 1

A cyclist rides 6.0 km east in 15 min, then 2.0 km west in 5.0 min. Find the average velocity and average speed for the whole trip, in km/h.

Total time: 20 min $= \tfrac13$ h. Displacement: $+6.0 - 2.0 = +4.0$ km (east). Distance: $6.0 + 2.0 = 8.0$ km.

Average velocity: $\dfrac{4.0\text{ km}}{1/3\text{ h}} = 12$ km/h east. Average speed: $\dfrac{8.0}{1/3} = 24$ km/h.

Notice you can't average the two legs' velocities ($24$ km/h and $-24$ km/h) to get the answer; average velocity always comes from total displacement over total time.

## Acceleration

**[[Acceleration]]** is the rate of change of velocity:

$$a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t},$$

with units m/s², read "meters per second, per second": each second the velocity changes by that many m/s. Its sign tells the direction of the change, not whether the object speeds up. An object speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs. A car moving in the $-x$ direction and braking has $v < 0$ and $a > 0$. Avoid the word "deceleration" in calculations; it hides the sign.

## Motion graphs

Graphs carry the same information as equations, often more clearly.

*Position–time ($x$–$t$) graph.* The slope at any point is the instantaneous velocity. A straight line means constant velocity; a curve means changing velocity. The slope of a chord between two points is the average velocity over that interval.

```plot
{"x": [0, 6], "y": [-1, 10], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "x (m)", "functions": [{"f": "0.5*x^2 - 0.5*x", "from": 0, "to": 5, "label": "x(t)"}], "tangents": [{"f": "0.5*x^2 - 0.5*x", "at": 3}], "points": [{"at": [3, 3], "label": "slope here = v(3) = 2.5 m/s"}], "caption": "An x–t graph curving upward: the slope (velocity) is increasing"}
```

*Velocity–time ($v$–$t$) graph.* Two facts make it the most useful kinematics graph:

1. The slope is the acceleration.
2. The signed area between the curve and the $t$ axis is the displacement. Area above the axis counts positive, below counts negative.

The area fact comes from $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$ for each thin strip of time: the strip's area is exactly its displacement, and adding strips adds displacements.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [-4, 8], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "v (m/s)", "functions": [{"f": "if(x < 4, 1.5*x, if(x < 7, 6, 6 - 4*(x - 7)))", "from": 0, "to": 9, "label": "v(t)"}], "shade": [{"f": "if(x < 4, 1.5*x, if(x < 7, 6, 6 - 4*(x - 7)))", "from": 0, "to": 9}], "caption": "Speeding up (0–4 s), constant velocity (4–7 s), then slowing, stopping at 8.5 s and reversing"}
```

*Acceleration–time ($a$–$t$) graph.* The area under it is the change in velocity, $\Delta v$.

### Example 2

Use the $v$–$t$ graph above. (a) What is the acceleration from 0 to 4 s? (b) What is the displacement from 0 to 7 s? (c) When does the object turn around?

(a) Slope $= \dfrac{6 - 0}{4 - 0} = 1.5$ m/s².

(b) Area: a triangle from 0 to 4 s, $\tfrac12(4)(6) = 12$ m, plus a rectangle from 4 to 7 s, $3(6) = 18$ m. Total 30 m.

(c) It turns around where $v$ changes sign. After 7 s, $v = 6 - 4(t - 7)$, which is zero at $t = 8.5$ s. Before 8.5 s it moves in $+x$, after it in $-x$. Note that $a = -4$ m/s² throughout the last segment, including the instant $v = 0$: the object is momentarily at rest but still accelerating.

## Velocity and acceleration as derivatives

Instantaneous quantities are derivatives. Velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration the derivative of velocity:

$$v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}, \qquad a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}.$$

These are the "slope of the graph" statements made exact. Going the other way, the "area under the graph" statements are integrals:

$$x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t v(t')\,dt', \qquad v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a(t')\,dt'.$$

The initial values $x_0$ and $v_0$ are the constants of integration: knowing the acceleration alone doesn't tell you where the object started or how fast it was going.

### Example 3

A particle moves along $x$ with $x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ (meters, seconds). Find its velocity and acceleration at $t = 3$ s, and the times when it is momentarily at rest.

Differentiate: $v(t) = 6t^2 - 18t + 12$ and $a(t) = 12t - 18$.

At $t = 3$: $v = 54 - 54 + 12 = 12$ m/s and $a = 36 - 18 = 18$ m/s².

At rest when $v = 0$: $6(t^2 - 3t + 2) = 6(t - 1)(t - 2) = 0$, so $t = 1$ s and $t = 2$ s. Between them $v < 0$ (try $t = 1.5$: $v = -1.5$ m/s), so the particle moves forward, backs up between 1 and 2 s, then moves forward again.

### Example 4

A drag racer's acceleration is $a(t) = 12 - 2t$ m/s² for $0 \le t \le 6$ s, starting from rest at $x = 0$. Find its velocity and position at $t = 6$ s.

$v(t) = \int_0^t (12 - 2t')\,dt' = 12t - t^2$, so $v(6) = 72 - 36 = 36$ m/s.

$x(t) = \int_0^t (12t' - t'^2)\,dt' = 6t^2 - \tfrac13 t^3$, so $x(6) = 216 - 72 = 144$ m.

The constant-acceleration formulas of the next lesson would be wrong here, because $a$ changes with time.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing distance with displacement, or speed with velocity.
- Reading an $x$–$t$ graph's height as the velocity; velocity is the slope.
- Thinking negative acceleration always means slowing down.
- Thinking $v = 0$ means $a = 0$ (a ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$ but $a = -9.8$ m/s²).
- Averaging velocities from legs of unequal duration.

## Key points

- Displacement $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ is signed; distance is not.
- $v_{\text{avg}} = \Delta x/\Delta t$; $a_{\text{avg}} = \Delta v/\Delta t$.
- Slope of $x$–$t$ is $v$; slope of $v$–$t$ is $a$; area under $v$–$t$ is $\Delta x$; area under $a$–$t$ is $\Delta v$.
- $v = dx/dt$, $a = dv/dt$; integrate (with initial conditions) to go back.

lessons.title: Constant acceleration and free fall
lessons.body:
## The most useful special case

Last lesson defined velocity and acceleration in general. Most textbook problems, and a surprising amount of real life (a braking car, a dropped phone, a ball thrown upward), involve acceleration that stays constant. In that case the general relationships collapse into four short equations, and a whole family of problems becomes a matter of choosing the right one.

## The four kinematic equations

Suppose $a$ is constant, the clock starts at $t = 0$ with position $x_0$ and velocity $v_0$. Since the $v$–$t$ graph is a straight line with slope $a$,

$$v = v_0 + at. \tag{1}$$

The displacement is the area under that line: a rectangle $v_0 t$ plus a triangle $\tfrac12(at)t$:

$$x - x_0 = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2. \tag{2}$$

Because $v$ changes linearly, the average velocity is the average of the end values, $\tfrac12(v_0 + v)$, so

$$x - x_0 = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)\,t. \tag{3}$$

Eliminating $t$ between (1) and (2) gives a time-free equation:

$$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0). \tag{4}$$

Each equation leaves out one of the five quantities $\Delta x, v_0, v, a, t$: (1) has no $\Delta x$, (2) no $v$, (3) no $a$, (4) no $t$. So the strategy is: list the three you know and the one you want, then pick the equation missing the fifth.

These equations are valid only while $a$ is constant. If a car accelerates and then brakes, treat each phase separately, using the final velocity of the first phase as the initial velocity of the second.

### Example 1

A car moving at 25 m/s brakes with constant acceleration of magnitude 5.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping, and how long does it take?

Take $+x$ along the motion. Known: $v_0 = 25$ m/s, $v = 0$, $a = -5.0$ m/s². Want $\Delta x$ (no $t$ given), so use (4):

$$0 = 25^2 + 2(-5.0)\Delta x \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta x = \frac{625}{10} = 62.5\text{ m}.$$

For the time, (1): $0 = 25 - 5.0t$, so $t = 5.0$ s.

Note how stopping distance scales with $v_0^2$: doubling the speed quadruples the stopping distance. That is why speed limits near schools are so low.

## Free fall

Near Earth's surface, with air resistance neglected, every object accelerates downward at the same rate, the **[[acceleration due to gravity]]**, $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ (more precisely 9.81 at sea level; it varies slightly with location). An object moving under gravity alone is in **[[free fall]]**, whether it's dropped, thrown up, or thrown down. A feather and a hammer fall together on the Moon, where there's no air.

With $+y$ pointing up, free fall is constant acceleration with $a = -g$:

$$v_y = v_{0y} - gt, \qquad y = y_0 + v_{0y}t - \tfrac12 g t^2, \qquad v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2g(y - y_0).$$

The value $g$ is a positive number; the minus sign comes from choosing up as positive. You may choose down as positive instead, but then use it consistently for every quantity.

### Example 2

A ball is thrown straight up at 14.7 m/s from the edge of a roof 20.0 m above the ground. Find (a) its maximum height above the roof, (b) the time to reach it, and (c) its speed just before hitting the ground. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s².

(a) At the top, $v_y = 0$. Time-free equation: $0 = 14.7^2 - 2(9.8)\,\Delta y$, so $\Delta y = \dfrac{216.09}{19.6} = 11.0$ m above the roof.

(b) $0 = 14.7 - 9.8t$, so $t = 1.5$ s.

(c) From launch to ground, $\Delta y = -20.0$ m (it ends below where it started):

$$v_y^2 = 14.7^2 - 2(9.8)(-20.0) = 216.09 + 392 = 608.09,$$

so the speed is $\sqrt{608.09} = 24.7$ m/s (and $v_y = -24.7$ m/s, downward).

A useful symmetry: when the ball comes back down past the roof, it has the same speed it was thrown with, 14.7 m/s, and the time up equals the time down.

### Example 3

A stone is dropped into a well and the splash is heard 2.50 s later. Ignoring the time for sound to travel up, how deep is the well, and how fast is the stone moving at the bottom?

Dropped means $v_{0y} = 0$. Take down as positive to avoid signs: $d = \tfrac12 g t^2 = \tfrac12(9.8)(2.50)^2 = 30.6$ m, and $v = gt = 24.5$ m/s. (Sound at about 343 m/s takes roughly 0.09 s to climb 30 m, so the true depth is a bit less; a good example of checking whether a neglected effect is really small.)

## Graphs of constant-acceleration motion

With constant $a$: the $a$–$t$ graph is a horizontal line, the $v$–$t$ graph is a straight line of slope $a$, and the $x$–$t$ graph is a parabola. For a ball thrown upward, $y(t)$ is an upside-down parabola whose peak is where the $v$–$t$ line crosses zero.

```plot
{"x": [0, 3.2], "y": [-18, 18], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "y (m), v (m/s)", "functions": [{"f": "14.7*x - 4.9*x^2", "from": 0, "to": 3}, {"f": "14.7 - 9.8*x", "from": 0, "to": 3, "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [1.5, 11.025], "label": "top: v = 0"}], "labels": [{"at": [2.75, 7], "text": "y(t)"}, {"at": [2.35, -12], "text": "v(t)"}], "caption": "Thrown up at 14.7 m/s: position is a parabola, velocity a straight line of slope −9.8 m/s²"}
```

## The equations from integration

Constant acceleration is the simplest case of integrating $a(t)$. With $a$ constant,

$$v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a\,dt' = v_0 + at, \qquad x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t (v_0 + at')\,dt' = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac12at^2.$$

Equation (4) also falls out of calculus using the chain rule: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$, so $a\,dx = v\,dv$. Integrating both sides from start to finish gives $a(x - x_0) = \tfrac12(v^2 - v_0^2)$. The identity $a = v\,dv/dx$ is worth remembering: it solves problems where acceleration depends on position rather than time.

When air resistance matters, acceleration is no longer constant: a falling object approaches a **[[terminal velocity]]** at which drag balances its weight. We'll set up and solve that differential equation in the friction lesson, once we have Newton's laws.

## Common mistakes

- Using the constant-acceleration equations when $a$ changes (for example across a braking phase and a coasting phase together).
- Writing $g = -9.8$ and then also putting a minus sign in front of $g$, double-counting the direction.
- Setting $a = 0$ at the top of a throw; only $v_y$ is zero there.
- Forgetting that $\Delta y$ is negative when the object ends below its start.
- Solving the quadratic (2) and keeping the negative time root.

## Key points

- For constant $a$: $v = v_0 + at$, $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$, $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t$, $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$.
- Pick the equation that omits the one quantity you neither know nor want.
- Free fall: $a = -g$ with up positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s², regardless of mass.
- Stopping distance grows with the square of speed.

lessons.title: Projectile motion
lessons.body:
## Two motions at once

A thrown ball, a long jumper, water from a hose: once released, each moves under gravity alone. This is **[[projectile motion]]**, and it is the payoff of the previous two lessons. The key idea is that horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Gravity pulls only down, so it changes only the vertical velocity; the horizontal velocity stays constant (ignoring air resistance). A projectile is just a constant-velocity problem in $x$ running side by side with a free-fall problem in $y$, and the two share one thing: the clock.

A famous demonstration: drop one ball and, at the same instant, fire another horizontally from the same height. They hit the floor together. The horizontal motion doesn't delay or speed up the fall.

## The equations

Put the origin at the launch point with $+y$ up. If the launch speed is $v_0$ at angle $\theta$ above horizontal, the initial components are

$$v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta, \qquad v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta.$$

Then for all later times (until it lands),

$$x = v_{0x}t, \qquad v_x = v_{0x},$$
$$y = v_{0y}t - \tfrac12gt^2, \qquad v_y = v_{0y} - gt.$$

Eliminating $t$ ($t = x/v_{0x}$) gives $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}x^2$, a downward parabola. That's why every projectile path, from a basketball shot to a fountain's arc, is parabolic.

The speed at any moment is $\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$, and the velocity is always tangent to the path.

## Horizontal launches

When $\theta = 0$, $v_{0y} = 0$: the object starts falling from rest vertically while sliding along horizontally. The fall time depends only on the height, and the horizontal distance is speed times that time.

### Example 1

A ball rolls off a table 1.20 m high at 3.0 m/s. Where does it land, and how fast is it moving at impact? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s².

Vertical (take down as positive here): $1.20 = \tfrac12(9.8)t^2$, so $t = \sqrt{2(1.20)/9.8} = 0.495$ s.

Horizontal: $x = 3.0 \times 0.495 = 1.48$ m from the table's edge.

Impact velocity: $v_x = 3.0$ m/s, $v_y = gt = 4.85$ m/s downward. Speed $= \sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.85^2} = 5.70$ m/s, at $\tan^{-1}(4.85/3.0) = 58^\circ$ below horizontal.

## Launches at an angle

For a launch from level ground that lands at the same height, three results are worth knowing (and deriving):

- *Time of flight.* $y = 0$ again when $v_{0y}t - \tfrac12gt^2 = 0$, so $T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$.
- *Maximum height.* At the top $v_y = 0$; from $v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2gH$: $H = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$.
- *Range.* $R = v_{0x}T = \dfrac{2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g} = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$.

The range is largest when $\sin 2\theta = 1$, that is $\theta = 45^\circ$. Complementary angles ($30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, say) give the same range, since $\sin 2\theta = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta)$; the steeper shot goes higher and stays up longer.

```plot
{"x": [0, 45], "y": [0, 20], "equal": true, "xLabel": "x (m)", "yLabel": "y (m)", "functions": [{"f": "x*tand(30) - 9.8*x^2/(2*400*cosd(30)^2)", "from": 0, "to": 35.35}, {"f": "x - 9.8*x^2/400", "from": 0, "to": 40.82}, {"f": "x*tand(60) - 9.8*x^2/(2*400*cosd(60)^2)", "from": 0, "to": 35.35}], "labels": [{"at": [17.7, 6.2], "text": "30°"}, {"at": [20.4, 11.2], "text": "45°"}, {"at": [17.7, 16.4], "text": "60°"}], "caption": "Launched at 20 m/s: 45° goes farthest; 30° and 60° land at the same spot"}
```

These shortcut formulas hold only when the projectile lands at its launch height. For a cliff, a basket above the shooter, or a ball hit from a tee into a hill, go back to the component equations.

### Example 2

A soccer ball is kicked at 18.0 m/s at $35^\circ$ above level ground. Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the range.

Components: $v_{0x} = 18.0\cos 35^\circ = 14.74$ m/s, $v_{0y} = 18.0\sin 35^\circ = 10.32$ m/s.

Time of flight: $T = 2(10.32)/9.8 = 2.11$ s.

Maximum height: $H = \dfrac{10.32^2}{2(9.8)} = 5.44$ m.

Range: $R = 14.74 \times 2.107 = 31.1$ m. Check with the formula: $R = \dfrac{18.0^2\sin 70^\circ}{9.8} = \dfrac{324(0.9397)}{9.8} = 31.1$ m.

### Example 3

A stone is thrown from a cliff 25.0 m high at 15.0 m/s, $30^\circ$ above horizontal. How long until it hits the water below, and how far from the cliff base?

Here the range formula doesn't apply. Components: $v_{0x} = 13.0$ m/s, $v_{0y} = 7.50$ m/s. Origin at the launch point, up positive; the water is at $y = -25.0$ m:

$$-25.0 = 7.50t - 4.9t^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 4.9t^2 - 7.50t - 25.0 = 0.$$

Quadratic formula: $t = \dfrac{7.50 + \sqrt{56.25 + 490}}{9.8} = \dfrac{7.50 + 23.37}{9.8} = 3.15$ s (the other root is negative, before the throw).

Horizontal distance: $x = 13.0 \times 3.15 = 40.9$ m.

## Vector form and air resistance

In vector form, the projectile has constant acceleration $\vec a = -g\,\hat\jmath$. Integrating once and twice,

$$\vec v(t) = \vec v_0 - gt\,\hat\jmath, \qquad \vec r(t) = \vec r_0 + \vec v_0t - \tfrac12gt^2\,\hat\jmath,$$

which is the component equations in one line. Calculus also confirms the optimal angle: $\dfrac{dR}{d\theta} = \dfrac{2v_0^2\cos 2\theta}{g} = 0$ gives $\theta = 45^\circ$. With air drag proportional to velocity, $\vec a = -g\hat\jmath - (b/m)\vec v$, the equations become differential equations whose solutions decay exponentially toward a terminal velocity; the path is no longer a parabola, it falls more steeply on the way down, and the best angle drops below $45^\circ$.

## Common mistakes

- Letting gravity affect $v_x$, or forgetting that $v_x$ stays constant.
- Using $v_0$ instead of $v_0\cos\theta$ for horizontal motion (or $\sin$ and $\cos$ swapped).
- Using the range formula when launch and landing heights differ.
- Saying the speed at the top is zero; only $v_y$ is zero there, and $v_x$ is unchanged.
- Treating the time to reach the top as the whole flight time.

## Key points

- Horizontal: constant velocity $v_0\cos\theta$. Vertical: free fall with $v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$. Time links them.
- Level ground: $T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$, $H = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ (max at $45^\circ$).
- Other launch and landing heights: solve the $y$ equation for $t$, then use it in $x$.

lessons.title: Motion in two dimensions and relative motion
lessons.body:
## Beyond the straight line

Projectiles showed that two-dimensional motion splits into independent one-dimensional motions. This lesson makes that idea general, using position, velocity and acceleration vectors, and then tackles a question that matters to every pilot, sailor and swimmer: how does motion look from a frame of reference that is itself moving?

## Position, velocity and acceleration vectors

In two dimensions the position is a vector $\vec r = x\,\hat\imath + y\,\hat\jmath$. Over a time interval the displacement is $\Delta\vec r = \vec r_f - \vec r_i$, and

$$\vec v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\vec r}{\Delta t}, \qquad \vec a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\vec v}{\Delta t}.$$

Each is computed component by component: $v_{\text{avg},x} = \Delta x/\Delta t$, and so on.

A subtle but important point: acceleration is any change in the velocity vector, including a change in direction only. A car rounding a curve at a steady 50 km/h is accelerating, because its velocity vector is turning. The acceleration then has two parts:

- a **[[tangential]]** part, along the velocity, which changes the speed;
- a **[[radial]]** (centripetal) part, perpendicular to the velocity, which changes the direction.

We'll study the second one in detail in the circular-motion lesson.

### Example 1

A boat at the origin moves to $(120\text{ m}, 50\text{ m})$ in 20 s. Its velocity changes from $(4.0, 0)$ m/s to $(5.0, 4.0)$ m/s over the same time. Find the average velocity and average acceleration.

$\vec v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{(120, 50)}{20} = (6.0, 2.5)$ m/s, magnitude $\sqrt{36 + 6.25} = 6.5$ m/s.

$\vec a_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{(5.0 - 4.0,\ 4.0 - 0)}{20} = (0.050, 0.20)$ m/s², magnitude $0.206$ m/s². The average acceleration points mostly sideways to the boat's original heading: over these 20 s the boat turns through $39^\circ$ as well as speeding up from 4.0 to 6.4 m/s.

## Relative motion

Velocity is always measured relative to something. A passenger walking forward at 1.5 m/s on a train moving at 30 m/s has velocity 1.5 m/s relative to the train and 31.5 m/s relative to the ground. Each observer uses a **[[reference frame]]**, a set of axes attached to some object.

The rule for combining velocities uses a subscript notation that almost checks itself. Write $\vec v_{AB}$ for "velocity of A relative to B". Then

$$\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}.$$

The inner subscripts match and "cancel," like conversion factors. Also $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$: if you see a car approaching you at 20 m/s, its driver sees you approaching at 20 m/s in the opposite direction. This is **[[relative velocity]]**, and it is just vector addition.

The rule works because positions add: if A is at $\vec r_{AB}$ relative to B and B at $\vec r_{BC}$ relative to C, then $\vec r_{AC} = \vec r_{AB} + \vec r_{BC}$; differentiate with respect to time and the velocities add the same way. (Einstein showed this fails at speeds near light; special relativity is covered in University Physics II.)

### Example 2: crossing a river

A river 80 m wide flows east at 1.2 m/s. A swimmer can swim at 2.0 m/s relative to the water. (a) If she heads straight across (north), how long does it take and how far downstream does she land? (b) Which way must she head to land directly opposite her start, and how long does that take?

Let S = swimmer, W = water, G = ground. $\vec v_{SG} = \vec v_{SW} + \vec v_{WG}$.

(a) $\vec v_{SW} = (0, 2.0)$, $\vec v_{WG} = (1.2, 0)$, so $\vec v_{SG} = (1.2, 2.0)$ m/s. Crossing time comes from the northward component alone: $t = 80/2.0 = 40$ s. Downstream drift: $1.2 \times 40 = 48$ m.

(b) To land opposite, $\vec v_{SG}$ must point due north, so the east component of $\vec v_{SW}$ must cancel the current: $2.0\sin\alpha = 1.2$, giving $\alpha = 36.9^\circ$ west of north (upstream). Her northward speed is then $2.0\cos 36.9^\circ = 1.6$ m/s, and the crossing takes $80/1.6 = 50$ s.

```shape
{"x": [-2.7, 2.0], "y": [-0.2, 1.95], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [-1.2, 1.6], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-1.2, 1.6], "to": [0, 1.6], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [0, 1.6], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [-1.55, 0.7], "text": "swimmer/water 2.0 m/s"}, {"at": [-0.6, 1.75], "text": "water/ground 1.2 m/s"}, {"at": [1.08, 0.8], "text": "swimmer/ground 1.6 m/s"}], "caption": "Heading upstream so the resultant points straight across"}
```

Heading straight across is the fastest way over; heading upstream is the way to land opposite. These are different goals with different answers, and the swimmer can land opposite only if her speed relative to the water exceeds the current's.

### Example 3: airplane in a crosswind

A plane flies with airspeed 220 km/h and must travel due north. A wind blows from west to east at 50 km/h. Find the heading and the ground speed.

$\vec v_{PG} = \vec v_{PA} + \vec v_{AG}$, with $\vec v_{AG} = (50, 0)$. For $\vec v_{PG}$ to point north, $220\sin\alpha = 50$, so $\alpha = 13.1^\circ$ west of north. Ground speed: $220\cos 13.1^\circ = \sqrt{220^2 - 50^2} = 214$ km/h.

## Velocity and acceleration as derivatives

For any motion in two or three dimensions,

$$\vec v = \frac{d\vec r}{dt} = \frac{dx}{dt}\hat\imath + \frac{dy}{dt}\hat\jmath, \qquad \vec a = \frac{d\vec v}{dt},$$

differentiating each component separately (the unit vectors are constant). Integration goes the other way, one component at a time, using the initial position and velocity.

### Example 4

A particle has $\vec r(t) = (3t^2)\,\hat\imath + (8t - t^3)\,\hat\jmath$ m. Find its velocity, speed and acceleration at $t = 2$ s.

$\vec v = 6t\,\hat\imath + (8 - 3t^2)\,\hat\jmath$, so $\vec v(2) = 12\hat\imath - 4\hat\jmath$ m/s and the speed is $\sqrt{144 + 16} = 12.6$ m/s.

$\vec a = 6\,\hat\imath - 6t\,\hat\jmath$, so $\vec a(2) = 6\hat\imath - 12\hat\jmath$ m/s².

The tangential part of the acceleration is the component along $\vec v$: $\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec v}{|\vec v|} = \dfrac{72 + 48}{12.65} = 9.49$ m/s². The particle is speeding up at that rate; the rest of $\vec a$ is turning it.

Differentiating the velocity-addition rule $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$ gives a result about accelerations: if frame B moves at constant velocity relative to frame C, then $\vec a_{AC} = \vec a_{AB}$. Observers in frames moving uniformly relative to each other measure the same accelerations, which is why Newton's laws hold equally in all such **[[inertial frames]]**.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking constant speed means zero acceleration (direction changes count).
- Adding relative velocities as magnitudes instead of vectors.
- Getting the subscript order wrong ($\vec v_{AB}$ vs $\vec v_{BA}$ differ by a sign).
- Using the swimmer's speed relative to water for the crossing time when she heads upstream; only the component across the river counts.

## Key points

- $\vec v_{\text{avg}} = \Delta\vec r/\Delta t$, $\vec a_{\text{avg}} = \Delta\vec v/\Delta t$, computed by components.
- Acceleration includes changes of direction; tangential changes speed, radial changes direction.
- Relative velocity: $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$ and $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$.
- $\vec v = d\vec r/dt$, $\vec a = d\vec v/dt$ component by component.

lessons.title: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams
lessons.body:
## From describing motion to explaining it

Kinematics told us how to describe motion. Dynamics asks why objects move the way they do, and Newton's three laws answer that for everything from falling apples to orbiting satellites. The central quantity is **[[force]]**: a push or pull exerted by one object on another, measured in newtons (N). Forces are vectors, so all the component methods from the vectors lesson come straight back.

## Newton's first law

An object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net force acts on it. This is **[[Newton's first law]]**, the law of **[[inertia]]**: the tendency of matter to keep its current velocity. A hockey puck sliding on ice slows only because of small friction forces; with none, it would glide forever.

The first law corrects an intuition many people hold: that motion needs a force to sustain it. It doesn't. A force is needed to *change* motion. The law also defines the frames we work in: it holds in inertial frames (non-accelerating ones). In an accelerating car, a coffee cup slides backward with no force pushing it; that's the car accelerating out from under it.

## Newton's second law

The **[[net force]]** $\vec F_{\text{net}} = \sum\vec F$ is the vector sum of all forces on an object. **[[Newton's second law]]** says

$$\sum \vec F = m\vec a.$$

The acceleration points the same way as the net force, and the **[[mass]]** $m$ measures how strongly the object resists acceleration. The same push gives a shopping cart a large acceleration and a car a tiny one. This is also where the newton comes from: 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

Because it is a vector equation, it is really one equation per axis:

$$\sum F_x = ma_x, \qquad \sum F_y = ma_y.$$

If the net force is zero, $\vec a = 0$, and the object is in **[[equilibrium]]** (at rest, or moving at constant velocity; both count).

## Weight and the normal force

The **[[weight]]** of an object is the gravitational force Earth exerts on it, $\vec W = m\vec g$, magnitude $mg$, pointing down. Mass is in kilograms and is the same everywhere; weight is a force in newtons and depends on the local $g$. A 70 kg astronaut weighs 686 N on Earth and about 113 N on the Moon, where $g = 1.62$ m/s², but her mass is 70 kg in both places.

When an object presses on a surface, the surface pushes back perpendicular to itself. This is the **[[normal force]]** $\vec n$ ("normal" means perpendicular). It is whatever size is needed to stop the object sinking into the surface, so don't assume $n = mg$; find it from Newton's second law in the perpendicular direction. A book on a flat table has $n = mg$, but push down on the book and $n$ grows; tilt the table and $n$ shrinks.

## Newton's third law

Forces come in pairs. If object A exerts a force on B, then B exerts a force on A of equal magnitude and opposite direction:

$$\vec F_{\text{A on B}} = -\vec F_{\text{B on A}}.$$

This is **[[Newton's third law]]**. The two forces of a pair act on *different* objects, so they never cancel each other in a single object's free-body diagram. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you equally. When Earth pulls a falling apple down with force $mg$, the apple pulls Earth up with force $mg$; Earth's enormous mass makes its acceleration immeasurably small.

A classic confusion: the weight of a book on a table and the normal force on the book are equal and opposite, but they are not a third-law pair. They act on the same object (the book), and they are different kinds of force. The third-law partner of the book's weight is the book's pull on Earth; the partner of the normal force is the book pushing down on the table.

## Free-body diagrams

A **[[free-body diagram]]** (FBD) isolates one object and shows every force acting *on* it, as arrows starting from the object. It is the single most important step in a dynamics problem. A reliable method:

1. Choose the object (or system) and draw it as a dot or simple box.
2. Draw its weight, $mg$ downward.
3. Go around the object's boundary: everything touching it can exert a force (normal force, friction, tension in an attached rope, an applied push).
4. Add any non-contact forces (electric, magnetic) if relevant.
5. Choose axes, ideally with one along the acceleration.
6. Write $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$, and solve.

Never put "$ma$" on the diagram as a force; it's the result of the forces, not one of them.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[-0.5, -0.5], [0.5, -0.5], [0.5, 0.5], [-0.5, 0.5]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0.5], "to": [0, 2.2], "arrow": true, "label": "n"}, {"from": [0, -0.5], "to": [0, -2.2], "arrow": true, "label": "mg"}, {"from": [0.5, 0], "to": [2.4, 0], "arrow": true, "label": "F (applied)"}, {"from": [-0.5, 0], "to": [-1.4, 0], "arrow": true, "label": "f (friction)"}], "caption": "Free-body diagram of a box pushed across a floor"}
```

### Example 1

A 12 kg crate on a frictionless floor is pulled by a rope with tension 60 N directed $30^\circ$ above horizontal. Find the acceleration and the normal force.

Forces on the crate: weight $mg = 117.6$ N down, normal force $n$ up, tension 60 N at $30^\circ$.

$x$: $60\cos 30^\circ = 12a$, so $a = \dfrac{51.96}{12} = 4.33$ m/s².

$y$: the crate doesn't leave the floor, so $a_y = 0$: $n + 60\sin 30^\circ - 117.6 = 0$, giving $n = 117.6 - 30 = 87.6$ N. The upward pull of the rope reduces the normal force.

### Example 2: apparent weight in an elevator

A 60 kg person stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator. What does the scale read when the elevator (a) accelerates upward at 2.0 m/s², (b) moves up at constant speed, (c) accelerates downward at 2.0 m/s²?

The scale reads the normal force $n$ it exerts. Take up as positive: $n - mg = ma$, so $n = m(g + a)$.

(a) $n = 60(9.8 + 2.0) = 708$ N, heavier than her true weight of 588 N.

(b) $a = 0$, so $n = 588$ N. Constant velocity is equilibrium.

(c) $a = -2.0$: $n = 60(7.8) = 468$ N. If the cable snapped ($a = -g$), the scale would read zero: she would feel weightless, though gravity still acts on her fully. This **[[apparent weight]]** is what your body senses.

## The momentum form of the second law

Newton actually wrote the second law in terms of momentum $\vec p = m\vec v$:

$$\vec F_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec p}{dt}.$$

For constant mass this is $m\,d\vec v/dt = m\vec a$; the momentum form also handles rockets and conveyor belts where mass changes. Writing $a = dv/dt$ turns the second law into a differential equation for the motion, which we can solve when forces depend on time or velocity.

### Example 3

A 2.0 kg object starts from rest and feels a force $F(t) = 6t^2$ N along $x$. Find its velocity at $t = 3$ s.

$m\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 6t^2$, so $dv = 3t^2\,dt$. Integrating from 0: $v(t) = t^3$, and $v(3) = 27$ m/s. Using $F(3)/m = 27$ m/s² as if it were constant would badly overestimate.

For velocity-dependent drag $F = -bv$, the equation $m\,dv/dt = -bv$ gives $v = v_0e^{-bt/m}$: exponential decay, which the next lesson extends to falling objects and terminal velocity.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking a moving object must have a net force in its direction of motion.
- Assuming $n = mg$ in every problem.
- Treating weight and normal force as a third-law pair.
- Drawing forces that the object exerts on others in its own free-body diagram.
- Including "$ma$" or "the force of motion" as a force.

## Key points

- First law: no net force, no change in velocity. Second law: $\sum\vec F = m\vec a$, one equation per axis. Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs on different objects.
- Weight $= mg$ downward; the normal force is perpendicular to the surface and found from the equations.
- Always draw a free-body diagram before writing equations.
- $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$ is the general form; it becomes a differential equation for variable forces.

lessons.title: Friction and inclined planes
lessons.body:
## Why things stop

Push a book across a table and it slows to a stop. The first law says something must be acting on it, and that something is **[[friction]]**: a force that surfaces in contact exert parallel to their surfaces, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide). This lesson adds friction to Newton's second law and then puts it to work on the inclined plane, the standard testing ground for free-body diagrams.

## Kinetic and static friction

Microscopically, even polished surfaces are rough, and contact points form temporary bonds. Two empirical rules describe the result well enough for most purposes.

**[[Kinetic friction]]** acts when surfaces slide over each other. Its magnitude is

$$f_k = \mu_k n,$$

where $n$ is the normal force and $\mu_k$ is the **[[coefficient of kinetic friction]]**, a dimensionless number depending on the pair of surfaces (rubber on dry concrete is about 0.7, steel on ice about 0.02). It points opposite to the sliding velocity, and to a good approximation it doesn't depend on speed or contact area.

**[[Static friction]]** acts when surfaces are not sliding but something is trying to make them. It adjusts to whatever value keeps the surfaces stuck, up to a maximum:

$$f_s \le \mu_s n.$$

The **[[coefficient of static friction]]** $\mu_s$ is usually larger than $\mu_k$, which is why it takes more force to start a heavy box moving than to keep it moving. The key subtlety: $f_s = \mu_s n$ only at the verge of slipping. A box that you're pushing with 20 N without moving it has 20 N of static friction, no matter how large $\mu_s n$ is.

Friction depends on $n$, not on the weight. Pull up on a sled rope and $n$ drops, and so does the friction.

### Example 1

A 25 kg box rests on a floor with $\mu_s = 0.50$ and $\mu_k = 0.35$. (a) What horizontal force is needed to start it moving? (b) If you keep pushing with that force once it slides, what is its acceleration?

Normal force: $n = mg = 25(9.8) = 245$ N (no vertical forces besides $n$ and $mg$).

(a) Maximum static friction: $\mu_s n = 0.50(245) = 122.5$ N. You need just over 122.5 N.

(b) Once sliding, friction drops to $f_k = 0.35(245) = 85.75$ N. Net force: $122.5 - 85.75 = 36.75$ N, so $a = 36.75/25 = 1.47$ m/s².

## The inclined plane

An object on a ramp tilted at angle $\theta$ is the classic problem where good axes matter. Tilt the axes: $x$ along the slope (down the slope positive is often convenient), $y$ perpendicular to it. Then the normal force and friction lie along the axes, and only the weight needs splitting.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [6, 0], [6, 3.464]]}, {"points": [[3.118, 1.8], [3.81, 2.2], [3.41, 2.893], [2.718, 2.493]]}], "segments": [{"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [3.264, 0.346], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [2.398, 3.846], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [4.303, 2.946], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [2.398, 1.846], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}, {"from": [3.264, 2.346], "to": [4.13, 0.846], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [3.6, 0.6], "text": "mg"}, {"at": [2.2, 3.95], "text": "n"}, {"at": [4.55, 3.1], "text": "f"}, {"at": [1.65, 1.75], "text": "mg sin θ"}, {"at": [4.85, 0.75], "text": "mg cos θ"}, {"at": [1.2, 0.25], "text": "θ = 30°"}], "caption": "Block on a 30° incline: weight mg splits into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope (dashed); n balances mg cos θ and friction f points up the slope"}
```

The weight makes angle $\theta$ with the $-y$ axis (the same angle as the incline, because both pairs of lines are mutually perpendicular). So:

- component down the slope: $mg\sin\theta$;
- component into the slope: $mg\cos\theta$.

Check the limits: at $\theta = 0$ (flat) the down-slope part vanishes; at $\theta = 90^\circ$ (vertical) it's all of $mg$. If you get them backwards, these limits will catch it.

Perpendicular to the slope there's no acceleration, so $n = mg\cos\theta$ (with no other perpendicular forces).

*Frictionless incline.* Along the slope: $mg\sin\theta = ma$, so $a = g\sin\theta$, independent of mass.

*With kinetic friction*, sliding down: $mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta = ma$, so

$$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta).$$

Sliding up (after a push), friction also points down the slope: $a = -g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$, a larger deceleration.

*On the verge of slipping* with static friction, $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so

$$\tan\theta_{\max} = \mu_s.$$

That gives a simple way to measure $\mu_s$: tilt a board until the object just starts to slide and take the tangent of the angle.

### Example 2

A 4.0 kg block slides down a $35^\circ$ ramp with $\mu_k = 0.25$. Find its acceleration and the friction force.

$n = mg\cos 35^\circ = 4.0(9.8)(0.8192) = 32.1$ N, so $f_k = 0.25(32.1) = 8.03$ N up the slope.

$a = g(\sin 35^\circ - 0.25\cos 35^\circ) = 9.8(0.5736 - 0.2048) = 3.61$ m/s² down the slope.

Check using forces: $mg\sin 35^\circ = 22.5$ N down the slope, minus 8.03 N friction, leaves 14.45 N; divided by 4.0 kg gives 3.61 m/s².

### Example 3

A skier on a $20^\circ$ slope with $\mu_s = 0.10$: will she slide from rest?

$\tan 20^\circ = 0.364 > 0.10$, so static friction can't hold her and she starts sliding. A slope gentle enough to stand still on would need $\theta \le \tan^{-1}(0.10) = 5.7^\circ$.

## Drag and terminal velocity

Friction between solid surfaces is roughly constant, but fluid resistance (drag) grows with speed. For slow motion through a viscous fluid, the drag is roughly proportional to speed, $F_D = bv$. A falling object then obeys

$$m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - bv.$$

Separating variables and integrating from rest gives

$$v(t) = \frac{mg}{b}\left(1 - e^{-bt/m}\right).$$

As $t\to\infty$ the velocity approaches the terminal velocity $v_T = mg/b$, where drag balances weight and the net force is zero. The time constant $m/b$ sets how quickly it gets there: after one time constant it has reached $1 - e^{-1} = 63\%$ of $v_T$. For fast objects in air the drag is closer to $\tfrac12 C\rho Av^2$, giving $v_T = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$; a skydiver's terminal speed is about 55 m/s belly-down.

## Common mistakes

- Using $f_s = \mu_s n$ when the object isn't on the verge of slipping.
- Using $n = mg$ on an incline or when a force pulls at an angle.
- Swapping $\sin$ and $\cos$ in the weight components (check $\theta = 0$ and $90^\circ$).
- Pointing kinetic friction along the motion instead of against it.
- Thinking friction depends on contact area or speed (in this model it doesn't).

## Key points

- Kinetic: $f_k = \mu_k n$, opposite the sliding. Static: $f_s \le \mu_s n$, just enough to prevent sliding.
- On an incline: $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope, $mg\cos\theta$ into it; $n = mg\cos\theta$.
- Frictionless: $a = g\sin\theta$. Sliding down with friction: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.
- Verge of slipping: $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.
- Linear drag: $v(t) = v_T(1 - e^{-bt/m})$, $v_T = mg/b$.

lessons.title: Tension, pulleys, and connected objects
lessons.body:
## Objects that pull on each other

Real problems rarely involve one object. Trains pull carriages, cranes lift loads, elevators hang from cables. This lesson extends free-body diagrams to systems of connected objects, linked by ropes and pulleys, and introduces the force that travels along a rope.

## Tension

A rope or cable pulled taut exerts a pull, the **[[tension]]** $T$, on whatever is attached to each end. It always pulls (a rope can't push) and acts along the rope. In this course ropes are usually idealized:

- A **[[massless rope]]** has the same tension throughout. (Apply $F = ma$ to a small piece: with $m = 0$, the forces on its two ends must balance.)
- An **[[ideal pulley]]** (massless, frictionless) changes the direction of a rope without changing its tension.
- An inextensible rope makes the connected objects move together with the same speed and the same magnitude of acceleration.

Tension is not automatically equal to the weight hanging from the rope. It equals $mg$ only if the hanging object is in equilibrium.

### Example 1: a hanging sign

A 20 kg sign hangs from two cables, each making $40^\circ$ with the horizontal. Find the tension in each.

By symmetry both tensions are equal, $T$. Horizontal components cancel. Vertical: $2T\sin 40^\circ = mg = 196$ N, so $T = \dfrac{196}{2(0.6428)} = 152$ N.

Notice each cable carries more than half the weight. As the cables flatten toward horizontal, $\sin\theta \to 0$ and the tension grows without bound, which is why a clothesline can never be pulled perfectly straight with laundry on it.

## Strategy for connected objects

1. Draw a separate free-body diagram for each object.
2. Choose a positive direction for each object consistent with the motion of the system (if block A moves right when block B moves down, call right positive for A and down positive for B). Then all accelerations have the same sign and magnitude $a$.
3. Write $\sum F = ma$ along the motion for each object.
4. Solve the equations together for $a$ and the tensions.

A shortcut for finding $a$ alone: treat the whole chain as one system of total mass $M$. Tensions inside the system are internal forces that cancel in pairs, so only external forces drive it: $a = F_{\text{net, ext}}/M$.

## The Atwood machine

Two masses $m_1 > m_2$ hang on either side of an ideal pulley. Taking the direction in which $m_1$ falls as positive:

- $m_1$: $m_1 g - T = m_1 a$
- $m_2$: $T - m_2 g = m_2 a$

Adding eliminates $T$: $(m_1 - m_2)g = (m_1 + m_2)a$, so

$$a = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g, \qquad T = \frac{2m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g.$$

The tension lies between the two weights: smaller than $m_1g$ (so $m_1$ accelerates down) and larger than $m_2 g$ (so $m_2$ accelerates up). Checks: if $m_1 = m_2$, $a = 0$ and $T = mg$; if $m_2 = 0$, $a = g$ (free fall) and $T = 0$.

```shape
{"circles": [{"center": [0, 4], "r": 0.6}], "segments": [{"from": [-0.6, 4], "to": [-0.6, 1.5]}, {"from": [0.6, 4], "to": [0.6, 2.5]}, {"from": [-1.4, 1.4], "to": [-1.4, 0.4], "arrow": true, "label": "a"}, {"from": [1.4, 1.9], "to": [1.4, 2.9], "arrow": true, "label": "a"}], "polygons": [{"points": [[-1, 0.5], [-0.2, 0.5], [-0.2, 1.5], [-1, 1.5]]}, {"points": [[0.2, 1.8], [1, 1.8], [1, 2.5], [0.2, 2.5]]}], "labels": [{"at": [-0.6, 0.2], "text": "m₁"}, {"at": [0.6, 1.5], "text": "m₂"}], "caption": "Atwood machine: the heavier mass m₁ accelerates down, m₂ up, with the same magnitude a"}
```

### Example 2

In an Atwood machine, $m_1 = 5.0$ kg and $m_2 = 3.0$ kg. Find the acceleration and tension.

$a = \dfrac{5.0 - 3.0}{8.0}(9.8) = 2.45$ m/s². $T = \dfrac{2(5.0)(3.0)}{8.0}(9.8) = 36.75$ N.

Check with $m_2$: $T - m_2g = 36.75 - 29.4 = 7.35$ N $= 3.0(2.45)$ ✓.

## A block on a table pulled by a hanging mass

Block $m_1$ sits on a horizontal table with kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k$; a rope over a pulley at the table's edge connects it to hanging mass $m_2$. Positive direction: $m_1$ moves toward the pulley, $m_2$ moves down.

- $m_1$ (horizontal): $T - \mu_k m_1 g = m_1 a$
- $m_2$ (vertical): $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$

Adding: $a = \dfrac{m_2 - \mu_k m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\,g$. If $m_2 g$ can't overcome static friction ($m_2 < \mu_s m_1$), nothing moves.

### Example 3

$m_1 = 6.0$ kg on the table with $\mu_k = 0.20$; $m_2 = 2.0$ kg hanging. Find $a$ and $T$.

$a = \dfrac{2.0 - 0.20(6.0)}{8.0}(9.8) = \dfrac{0.8}{8.0}(9.8) = 0.98$ m/s².

From $m_2$: $T = m_2(g - a) = 2.0(9.8 - 0.98) = 17.64$ N. Check with $m_1$: $17.64 - 0.20(6.0)(9.8) = 17.64 - 11.76 = 5.88 = 6.0(0.98)$ ✓.

## Mechanical advantage

A movable pulley supported by two rope segments lets you lift a load with half the force: if the load $W$ hangs from a pulley held up by two strands of the same rope, $2T = W$ in equilibrium, so $T = W/2$. The price is distance: to raise the load 1 m, you pull 2 m of rope. Block-and-tackle systems multiply this further. (In energy terms, the work you do is the same; you'll see why in the work lesson.)

## Constraints and ropes with mass

Constraints between connected objects are really statements about derivatives. If a rope of fixed length $L$ connects blocks at positions $x_1$ and $x_2$ measured along the rope, then $x_1 + x_2 = L$ (plus constants), and differentiating twice gives $\ddot x_1 = -\ddot x_2$: equal and opposite accelerations in those coordinates. For a movable pulley, the constraint is $2y_{\text{load}} + y_{\text{end}} = \text{const}$, so the load's acceleration is half the rope end's. Writing the length constraint and differentiating is the safe way to handle complicated pulley systems.

A rope with mass is different: tension varies along it. A uniform rope of mass $M$ and length $L$ hanging vertically has tension $T(y) = \dfrac{M}{L}\,g\,y$ at a height $y$ above its bottom end, since that point supports the weight of the rope below it.

## Common mistakes

- Setting tension equal to the hanging weight when the system accelerates.
- Using inconsistent sign conventions for the two objects, which makes the accelerations seem to differ.
- Including tension when treating the whole system as one object (it's internal).
- Forgetting friction on the table block, or using $\mu_s$ when it's sliding.

## Key points

- Tension pulls along a rope; ideal ropes and pulleys keep it the same throughout.
- Draw a separate FBD for each object; use one consistent positive direction around the system.
- Atwood: $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$, $T = \dfrac{2m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$.
- Table and hanging mass: $a = \dfrac{m_2 - \mu_k m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g$.
- Whole-system shortcut: $a = F_{\text{ext}}/M_{\text{total}}$.

lessons.title: Uniform circular motion
lessons.body:
## Turning requires a force

A car rounding a bend, a satellite in orbit, a ball whirled on a string: each moves in a circle, and each is accelerating even if its speed never changes, because its velocity keeps changing direction. By Newton's second law, something must supply a net force. This lesson finds how large that acceleration is, where it points, and which real forces provide it.

## Describing circular motion

An object moving in a circle of radius $r$ at constant speed $v$ is in **[[uniform circular motion]]**. The time for one revolution is the **[[period]]** $T$, and the number of revolutions per second is the **[[frequency]]** $f = 1/T$ (unit hertz, Hz $=$ s$^{-1}$). Since one lap is a distance $2\pi r$,

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = 2\pi r f.$$

## Centripetal acceleration

The velocity is always tangent to the circle, and the acceleration points toward the center. It's called **[[centripetal acceleration]]** ("center-seeking"), with magnitude

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}.$$

*Why $v^2/r$?* In a short time $\Delta t$, the object moves through a small angle $\Delta\theta = v\Delta t/r$. Its velocity vector, of fixed length $v$, rotates through the same angle, so the change in velocity has magnitude $|\Delta\vec v| \approx v\,\Delta\theta = v^2\Delta t/r$. Dividing by $\Delta t$ gives $a = v^2/r$. And as $\Delta\theta \to 0$, $\Delta\vec v$ is perpendicular to $\vec v$, pointing inward.

```shape
{"x": [-1.6, 1.6], "y": [-1.25, 1.6], "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "segments": [{"from": [0.707, 0.707], "to": [0.0, 1.414], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0.707, 0.707], "to": [0.283, 0.283], "arrow": true}], "points": [[0, 0], [0.707, 0.707]], "labels": [{"at": [0.47, 1.2], "text": "v"}, {"at": [0.32, 0.6], "text": "a"}, {"at": [0, -0.2], "text": "center"}], "caption": "In uniform circular motion (here counterclockwise), velocity v is tangent and acceleration a points to the center"}
```

## Centripetal force is a role, not a new force

Newton's second law toward the center reads

$$\sum F_{\text{toward center}} = \frac{mv^2}{r}.$$

The left side is the net inward force from real, identifiable forces: tension, gravity, friction, the normal force, or a combination. "Centripetal force" is a job description for whatever force(s) do the turning; it never belongs on a free-body diagram as an extra arrow. When the inward force disappears (a string snaps), the object continues in a straight line along the tangent. It doesn't fly outward; "centrifugal force" is what you feel in the car's non-inertial frame, not a real force in an inertial one.

### Example 1: car on a flat curve

What is the maximum speed at which a car can round a flat curve of radius 50 m if $\mu_s = 0.80$ between tires and road?

The tires don't slide sideways, so static friction provides the inward force. Vertically, $n = mg$. At the limit, $f_s = \mu_s mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so

$$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{0.80(9.8)(50)} = 19.8\text{ m/s} \approx 71\text{ km/h}.$$

The mass cancels: a truck and a motorcycle have the same limit (with the same tires). On ice, with $\mu_s \approx 0.1$, the limit drops to 7 m/s.

## Banked curves

Highway engineers tilt curves so the normal force helps. On a frictionless curve banked at angle $\theta$, the normal force tilts toward the center. Vertically, $n\cos\theta = mg$; horizontally (toward the center), $n\sin\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing,

$$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}.$$

At this design speed no friction is needed at all. Faster than this, friction must act down the slope; slower, up the slope.

## Vertical circles

A roller coaster loop or a bucket swung overhead moves in a vertical circle, usually not at constant speed, but the inward equation still holds at each point.

At the *top*, both gravity and the normal force (or tension) point down, toward the center: $n + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The minimum speed to stay on the track is when $n = 0$:

$$v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}.$$

At the *bottom*, the normal force points up (toward the center) and gravity down: $n - mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $n = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, which is why riders feel pressed into their seats at the bottom.

### Example 2

A 0.50 kg bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.90 m. (a) What is the minimum speed at the top for the water to stay in? (b) If the speed at the bottom is 5.0 m/s, what tension does the arm supply there?

(a) $v_{\min} = \sqrt{9.8(0.90)} = 2.97$ m/s. At that speed gravity alone provides exactly the needed inward force, and the water is in free fall along the circle with the bucket.

(b) At the bottom: $T = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = 0.50(9.8) + \dfrac{0.50(25)}{0.90} = 4.9 + 13.9 = 18.8$ N.

### Example 3: conical pendulum

A 0.20 kg ball on a 1.0 m string swings in a horizontal circle with the string at $30^\circ$ from vertical. Find its speed and period.

Radius: $r = L\sin 30^\circ = 0.50$ m. Vertical: $T\cos 30^\circ = mg$. Inward: $T\sin 30^\circ = mv^2/r$. Dividing, $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v = \sqrt{rg\tan 30^\circ} = \sqrt{0.50(9.8)(0.577)} = 1.68$ m/s. Period: $T_{\text{period}} = 2\pi r/v = 1.87$ s.

## Circular motion as a vector function

Parametrize the motion: $\vec r(t) = r\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath + r\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath$, where $\omega = 2\pi/T$ is the angular speed (radians per second). Differentiating,

$$\vec v = -r\omega\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\imath + r\omega\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath, \qquad \vec a = -r\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\,\hat\imath - r\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\,\hat\jmath = -\omega^2\vec r.$$

So $|\vec v| = r\omega$, $\vec v\cdot\vec r = 0$ (tangent), and $\vec a$ points opposite to $\vec r$, toward the center, with magnitude $r\omega^2 = v^2/r$. This confirms the geometric argument exactly.

When the speed changes (nonuniform circular motion), the acceleration has a tangential part $a_t = dv/dt$ as well as the radial part $v^2/r$, and the total is $a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + (v^2/r)^2}$.

## Common mistakes

- Drawing a separate "centripetal force" arrow in a free-body diagram.
- Saying an object released from circular motion flies outward (it flies off along the tangent).
- Using $n = mg$ at the top or bottom of a vertical circle.
- Mixing up period and frequency, or forgetting to convert rpm to revolutions per second.

## Key points

- $v = 2\pi r/T$; $a_c = v^2/r$ toward the center.
- Real forces supply the inward net force: $\sum F_{\text{in}} = mv^2/r$.
- Flat curve: $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. Banked, frictionless: $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$.
- Top of a vertical loop: $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$. Bottom: $n = mg + mv^2/r$.
- In vector form, $\vec r(t)$ differentiated twice gives $\vec a = -\omega^2\vec r$.

lessons.title: Work and kinetic energy
lessons.body:
## A second way to solve mechanics problems

Newton's laws connect force to acceleration at each instant. That's powerful but sometimes clumsy: if a force changes along the path, or the path curves, tracking the acceleration moment by moment gets hard. Energy methods sidestep that. They relate forces acting over a *distance* to changes in *speed*, using scalars instead of vectors. This lesson defines work and kinetic energy and proves the theorem linking them; the next adds potential energy and conservation.

## Work done by a constant force

When a constant force $\vec F$ acts on an object that undergoes a displacement $\vec d$, the **[[work]]** done by that force is

$$W = Fd\cos\theta,$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec F$ and $\vec d$. Only the component of the force along the displacement does work. Work is a scalar measured in **[[joules]]** ($1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N·m}$).

The sign of work matters:

- $0 \le \theta < 90^\circ$: $W > 0$. The force helps the motion (pulling a sled forward).
- $\theta = 90^\circ$: $W = 0$. The force is perpendicular to the motion: the normal force on a block sliding across a floor, or the tension in a string whirling a ball in a circle, does no work.
- $90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$: $W < 0$. The force opposes the motion (friction on a sliding box, $\theta = 180^\circ$).

Note that holding a heavy bag still does zero work on it in the physics sense, however tiring it is: there's no displacement.

When several forces act, the **[[net work]]** is the sum of the work each one does, which equals the work done by the net force.

### Example 1

A 15 kg sled is pulled 20 m across level snow by a rope with tension 50 N at $25^\circ$ above horizontal. Kinetic friction is 30 N. Find the work done by each force and the net work.

- Tension: $W_T = 50(20)\cos 25^\circ = 906$ J.
- Friction (opposite the motion): $W_f = 30(20)\cos 180^\circ = -600$ J.
- Gravity and the normal force are perpendicular to the displacement: 0 J each.

Net work: $906 - 600 = 306$ J.

## Kinetic energy and the work–energy theorem

**[[Kinetic energy]]** is the energy of motion:

$$K = \tfrac12 mv^2.$$

It is a scalar, never negative, and also measured in joules. A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has $K = 200\,000$ J $= 200$ kJ.

The **[[work–energy theorem]]** says that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2.$$

*Why, for a constant force:* along the line of motion, $F_{\text{net}} = ma$ and $v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2ad$. Multiply the second equation by $\tfrac12 m$: $\tfrac12mv_f^2 - \tfrac12mv_i^2 = mad = F_{\text{net}}d = W_{\text{net}}$.

Positive net work speeds an object up, negative net work slows it down, zero net work leaves its speed unchanged (which is why uniform circular motion keeps a constant speed: the inward force does no work).

### Example 2

Continue Example 1. If the sled starts from rest, how fast is it moving after 20 m?

$W_{\text{net}} = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - 0$, so $v_f = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(306)}{15}} = 6.39$ m/s.

No acceleration or time was needed. The energy route is especially efficient when a question asks "how fast after a certain distance."

### Example 3

A 1200 kg car moving at 25 m/s skids to a stop with friction force 9000 N. How far does it skid?

$W_{\text{net}} = -9000\,d = 0 - \tfrac12(1200)(25)^2 = -375\,000$ J, so $d = 41.7$ m. Doubling the speed quadruples $K$ and so quadruples the stopping distance, matching the kinematics result.

## Work by a varying force

If the force changes as the object moves, $W = Fd$ no longer works directly. Graphically, the work done by a force along $x$ is the area under the $F$–$x$ graph, just as displacement is the area under a $v$–$t$ graph.

The most important example is a spring. An ideal spring stretched or compressed by $x$ from its natural length pulls back with force

$$F_{\text{spring}} = -kx,$$

called **[[Hooke's law]]**, where $k$ is the **[[spring constant]]** (N/m), a measure of stiffness. The minus sign means the force is a restoring force: it always points back toward equilibrium.

To stretch a spring slowly from 0 to $x$, you apply force $kx$, which grows linearly. The work you do is the area of a triangle with base $x$ and height $kx$:

$$W = \tfrac12 kx^2.$$

```plot
{"x": [0, 0.25], "y": [0, 110], "xLabel": "stretch x (m)", "yLabel": "applied force F (N)", "functions": [{"f": "400*x", "from": 0, "to": 0.2, "label": "F = kx"}], "shade": [{"f": "400*x", "from": 0, "to": 0.2}], "caption": "Work to stretch a spring (k = 400 N/m) by 0.20 m is the triangle area: ½(0.20)(80) = 8.0 J"}
```

## Work as an integral

For a force that varies along a path, divide the path into tiny steps $d\vec\ell$; each contributes $\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell$. Adding them is a line integral:

$$W = \int_{\text{path}} \vec F\cdot d\vec\ell, \qquad \text{in one dimension: } W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x)\,dx.$$

For the spring, the work done *by the spring* as it goes from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is

$$W_s = \int_{x_1}^{x_2}(-kx)\,dx = -\left(\tfrac12kx_2^2 - \tfrac12kx_1^2\right).$$

The work–energy theorem holds for any force, by the chain-rule identity $a = v\,dv/dx$:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \int F_{\text{net}}\,dx = \int m v\frac{dv}{dx}\,dx = \int_{v_i}^{v_f} mv\,dv = \tfrac12mv_f^2 - \tfrac12mv_i^2.$$

### Example 4

A force $F(x) = 3x^2 - 2x$ N acts on a particle along the $x$ axis. How much work does it do as the particle moves from $x = 1$ m to $x = 3$ m?

$$W = \int_1^3 (3x^2 - 2x)\,dx = \left[x^3 - x^2\right]_1^3 = (27 - 9) - (1 - 1) = 18\text{ J}.$$

## Common mistakes

- Using the full force instead of its component along the displacement.
- Forgetting that friction does negative work.
- Writing $W = kx^2$ or $W = kx \cdot x$ for a spring (the force grows from zero, hence the $\tfrac12$).
- Calling work a vector; it's a scalar, though it can be negative.
- Using $W = Fd$ for a force that changes with position.

## Key points

- $W = Fd\cos\theta$ for a constant force; perpendicular forces do no work.
- $K = \tfrac12mv^2$; work–energy theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$.
- Hooke's law $F = -kx$; work to stretch a spring by $x$ is $\tfrac12kx^2$.
- In general $W = \int\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell$, the area under the $F$–$x$ graph.

lessons.title: Potential energy, conservation of energy, and power
lessons.body:
## Stored energy

Lift a book and the work you do isn't lost: let go and gravity gives it back as kinetic energy. Compress a spring and it pushes your hand back when released. This stored energy of position is **[[potential energy]]**, and together with kinetic energy it gives us one of the most useful principles in physics: conservation of energy. Problems that would need calculus with Newton's laws, like the speed at the bottom of a curved slide, become a line of algebra.

## Conservative forces and potential energy

Some forces have a special property: the work they do on an object moving between two points depends only on the endpoints, not the path. These are **[[conservative forces]]**. Gravity and spring forces are conservative; friction is not (dragging a box along a longer path does more negative work).

For a conservative force we define a potential energy $U$ so that the work done by the force equals the decrease in $U$:

$$W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U.$$

**[[Gravitational potential energy]]** near Earth's surface: gravity does work $-mg\Delta y$ when an object rises by $\Delta y$, so

$$U_g = mgy,$$

measured from any convenient reference level ($y = 0$). Only changes in $U$ matter, so the choice of zero is yours; just keep it fixed during a problem.

**[[Elastic potential energy]]** of a spring stretched or compressed by $x$:

$$U_s = \tfrac12kx^2,$$

which equals the work needed to deform it (last lesson).

## Conservation of mechanical energy

**[[Mechanical energy]]** is $E = K + U$. Combining the work–energy theorem ($W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$) with $W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U$: if only conservative forces do work, $\Delta K = -\Delta U$, so

$$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.$$
