questions.explanation: The gas returns to its initial state, and internal energy is a state variable, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$. Hence $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}}$, the area enclosed by the cycle.

questions.stem: Three moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated at constant volume, raising the temperature by 50 K. How much heat is added?
questions.explanation: $Q = nC_V\Delta T = 3(\tfrac32)(8.314)(50) = 1871$ J; no work is done at constant volume. 3118 J uses $C_P$.

questions.stem: A monatomic gas ($\gamma = 5/3$) is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Its absolute temperature
questions.explanation: $TV^{\gamma - 1}$ is constant, so $T_f = T_i(8)^{2/3} = 4T_i$. Adiabatic compression heats a gas strongly (diesel ignition).

questions.stem: What is the maximum possible efficiency of an engine working between 600 K and 300 K?
An engine takes in 1500 J of heat per cycle and exhausts 1050 J. What is its efficiency?
A Carnot engine runs between 127°C and 7°C. Its efficiency is
questions.explanation: In kelvins: 400 K and 280 K. $e = 1 - 280/400 = 0.30$. Using Celsius ($1 - 7/127$) gives the impossible-looking 94%.

questions.stem: Which statement is a form of the second law of thermodynamics?
choices: No cyclic engine can convert heat entirely into work
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature
questions.explanation: That's the Kelvin–Planck statement; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir. Energy conservation is the first law.

questions.stem: A refrigerator removes 300 J of heat from its interior using 100 J of work. What is its coefficient of performance, and how much heat goes to the kitchen?
questions.explanation: $K = Q_C/W = 300/100 = 3.0$. Energy conservation: $Q_H = Q_C + W = 400$ J delivered to the kitchen.

questions.stem: A reservoir at 400 K absorbs 2000 J of heat. What is its entropy change?
questions.explanation: $\Delta S = Q/T = 2000/400 = +5.0$ J/K (positive because heat flows in).

questions.stem: When heat flows from a hot object to a cold object, the total entropy of the two
questions.explanation: The hot object loses $Q/T_H$, the cold one gains $Q/T_C$, and since $T_C < T_H$ the gain is larger. Irreversible processes always raise total entropy.

questions.stem: What is the entropy change of 0.20 kg of ice melting at 0°C? ($L_f = 3.34\times10^5$ J/kg)
questions.explanation: $\Delta S = mL_f/T = 0.20(3.34\times10^5)/273 = +245$ J/K. Using $T = 0$ (Celsius) would make it undefined; always use kelvins.

questions.stem: A heat pump delivers 4 J of heat to a house for each 1 J of electrical work. Does this violate energy conservation?
choices: No: it moves 3 J of heat from outdoors plus the 1 J of work indoors
Yes, unless it is a Carnot engine
No, because heat is not energy
questions.explanation: $Q_H = Q_C + W$: 3 J extracted from the cold outdoors plus 1 J of work. A coefficient of performance above 1 is allowed; an efficiency above 1 is not.

questions.stem: Using $\Delta S = \int dQ/T$, the entropy change when mass $m$ of water (specific heat $c$) is heated from $T_1$ to $T_2$ is
questions.explanation: $dQ = mc\,dT$, so $\Delta S = mc\int_{T_1}^{T_2}dT/T = mc\ln(T_2/T_1)$ (temperatures in kelvins).

cards.front: SI base units for length, mass, time, current
cm² to m² and cm³ to m³
cards.back: $1\text{ cm}^2 = 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$; $1\text{ cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$. Square or cube the factor.

cards.front: Prefixes: G, M, k, c, m, μ, n
Sig figs rule for multiplying and dividing
cards.back: Keep as many significant figures as the input with the fewest.

cards.front: Sig figs rule for adding and subtracting
cards.back: Keep as many decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places.
Zeros between nonzero digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point. Leading zeros never are.

cards.front: What can dimensional analysis catch, and what can't it?
cards.back: It catches wrong powers and missing quantities, but not wrong pure-number factors like 2 or π.

cards.front: Arguments of sin, exp, ln must be…
Components of a vector at angle θ from +x

cards.back: Add their components separately: $R_x = A_x + B_x$, $R_y = A_y + B_y$.
$\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$ (a scalar; zero when perpendicular).
$|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\phi$, perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule; $\vec B\times\vec A = -\vec A\times\vec B$.
Displacement $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ is signed (a vector); distance is total path length, always positive.

cards.front: When does an object speed up?
cards.back: When $v$ and $a$ have the same sign. Opposite signs: it slows down.

cards.front: Slope of a v–t graph; area under a v–t graph
Constant-acceleration equation with no final v
Stopping distance from speed $v_0$ at deceleration $a$
